title: A clinical update on Antibiotic Resistance Gram-negative bacteria in Malaysia- a review
authors: ['Fazlul MKK', 'Shah Samiur Rashid', 'Nazmul MHM', 'Zaidul I. S. M', 'Roesnita Baharudin', 'Aizi Nor Mazila Ramli']
abstract: Antibiotics are the wonder discoveries to combat microbes. For decades, multiple varieties of antibiotics have been used for therapeutic purposes in hospital settings and communities throughout the world. Unfortunately, bacteria have become resistant to commonly prescribed antibiotics. This review aims to explore the development, challenges, and the current state of antibiotic resistance available literature in Malaysia. This review aims to explore the development, challenges, and the current state of antibiotic resistance available literature in Malaysia. This review reiterates the antibiotic resistance among the gram-negative bacteria is increasing and they are becoming resistant to nearly all groups of antibiotics. The antibiotic treatments are minimal and hard to treat in multi-drug resistance bacterial infection, resulting in morbidity and mortality. The prevalence rate of antibiotic resistance from the literature suggests that educating patients and the public is essential to prevent and control the spread of antibiotic resistance. In particular, there is an urgent need for a surveillance system of regular monitoring on the microbiomes, the discovery of novel antibiotics and therapeutic application of antibiotics are mandatory.

title: Predicting Antibiotic Resistance Patterns Using Sentence-BERT: A Machine Learning Approach
authors: ['Mahmoud Alwakeel', 'Michael E. Yarrington', 'Rebekah H. Wrenn', 'Ethan Fang', 'Jian Pei', 'Anand Chowdhury', 'An-Kwok Ian Wong']
abstract: Antibiotic resistance poses a significant threat in in-patient settings with high mortality. Using MIMIC-III data, we generated Sentence-BERT embeddings from clinical notes and applied Neural Networks and XGBoost to predict antibiotic susceptibility. XGBoost achieved an average F1 score of 0.86, while Neural Networks scored 0.84. This study is among the first to use document embeddings for predicting antibiotic resistance, offering a novel pathway for improving antimicrobial stewardship.

title: Antibiotic resistance: a physicist's view
abstract: The problem of antibiotic resistance poses challenges across many disciplines. One such challenge is to understand the fundamental science of how antibiotics work, and how resistance to them can emerge. This is an area where physicists can make important contributions. Here, we highlight cases where this is already happening, and suggest directions for further physics involvement in antimicrobial research.

title: Reliable uncertainty estimate for antibiotic resistance classification with Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
abstract: Antibiotic resistance monitoring is of paramount importance in the face of this on-going global epidemic. Deep learning models trained with traditional optimization algorithms (e.g. Adam, SGD) provide poor posterior estimates when tested against out-of-distribution (OoD) antibiotic resistant/non-resistant genes. In this paper, we introduce a deep learning model trained with Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to classify antibiotic resistant genes. The model provides better uncertainty estimates when tested against OoD data compared to traditional optimization methods such as Adam.

title: Bifurcation analysis and global dynamics of a mathematical model of antibiotic resistance in hospitals
abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria has posed a grave threat to public health by causing a number of nosocomial infections in hospitals. Mathematical models have been used to study the transmission of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within a hospital and the measures to control antibiotic resistance in nosocomial pathogens. Studies presented in \cite{LBL,LB} have shown great value in understanding the transmission of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a hospital. However, their results are limited to numerical simulations of a few different scenarios without analytical analysis of the models in all biologically feasible parameter regions. Bifurcation analysis and identification of the global stability conditions are necessary to assess the interventions which are proposed to limit nosocomial infection and stem the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. In this paper we study the global dynamics of the mathematical model of antibiotic resistance in hospitals in \cite{LBL,LB}. The invasion reproduction number $\mathcal R_{ar}$ of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is introduced. We give the relationship of $\mathcal R_{ar}$ and two control reproduction numbers of sensitive bacteria and resistant bacteria ($\mathcal R_{sc}$ and $\mathcal R_{rc}$). More importantly, we prove that a backward bifurcation may occur at $\mathcal R_{ar}=1$ when the model includes superinfection which is not mentioned in \cite{LB}. That is, there exists a new threshold $\mathcal R_{ar}^c$, and if $\mathcal R_{ar}^c<\mathcal R_{ar}<1$, then the system can have two interior equilibria and it supports an interesting bistable phenomenon. This provides critical information on controlling the antibiotic-resistance in a hospital.

title: Antibiotic Resistance
Antibiotic resistance - Meet the challenge
Antibiotic Resistance
abstract: Antibacterial resistance threatens the ability of physicians to treat infections, reversing medical gains and increasing the probability of morbidity and mortality in infected patients. Decreased antibiotic efficacy also threatens advanced surgical procedures dependent on antibiotic effectiveness, such as organ and prosthetic transplants. Even simple procedures consider antibiotic prophylaxis to be a standard means of controlling surgical site infections. Despite the link between increased antibiotic use and resistance, a large fraction of antimicrobial use is inappropriate, particularly for acute respiratory tract infections. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is the most significant antibiotic-resistant pathogen, but new pathogens such as carbapenem-resistant enterobacteriaceae (CRE) are increasing in clinical significance. Antibiotic use and resistance is rising rapidly in developing countries, particularly India, China, and various African countries. The inappropriate use of antibiotics must be reduced, and incentives for the development of new antibiotics should be increased.

title: Spreading Antibiotic Resistance?
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter focuses on the genetics that underpin antibiotic resistance. The swapping and transfer of antibiotic resistance among bacterial species will be explained. In addition, the emergence of new antibiotic resistant strains will be described with respect to the evolutionary pressure that is provided by mankind's reliance on antibiotics. This evolutionary pressure will be mapped on to Darwin's concept of “survival of the fittest”, where an antibiotic resistant bacterium can be the fittest in certain situations.</jats:p>

First-line immune checkpoint inhibitors combined with targeted therapy for advanced renal cell carcinoma: a network meta-analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy of first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) combined with targeted therapy for advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and assess their cost-effectiveness from the perspective of the Chinese healthcare system. METHODS: Phase III randomized controlled trials comparing ICI-targeted combinations versus sunitinib as first-line treatment for advanced RCC were identified through systematic searches of PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library. A network meta-analysis (NMA) was performed to compare the hazard ratios (HRs) for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) among different regimens. The surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) was calculated to rank treatment efficacy. Based on the NMA results, a partitioned survival model was developed for the cost-effectiveness analysis. Using the sunitinib arm from the CheckMate 9ER trial as the reference, parametric survival models were fitted to extrapolate survival outcomes over a 20-year time horizon. HRs from the NMA were applied to derive survival curves for other interventions. The model cycle length was 6 weeks. Costs included drug acquisition, follow-up, adverse event management, subsequent therapy, and palliative care. Utility values were sourced from published literature. An incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) was calculated against a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of $40,332.35 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY). Sensitivity and scenario analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Seven trials involving 4,973 patients were included. The NMA showed that pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib ranked highest for PFS, whereas toripalimab plus axitinib ranked highest for OS. The cost-effectiveness analysis indicated that toripalimab plus axitinib yielded the greatest gains in life-years and QALYs, with the lowest ICER of $62,204.37 among all evaluated strategies. However, all regimens exceeded the WTP threshold of $40,332.35 per QALY. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that while toripalimab plus axitinib is the most efficacious first-line regimen for aRCC and offers the lowest ICER, none of the evaluated regimens are economically viable from the perspective of the Chinese healthcare system at the WTP threshold of $40,332.35 per QALY. title: Dendritic-cell-targeting adeno-associated virus as potent cancer vaccine carriers.
authors: ['Xin Wei', 'Xiang Li', 'Lixia Qi', 'Wenxuan Qiu', 'Yuxin Zhang', 'Liping Wu', 'Shutang Wei', 'Bofeng Luo', 'Menghan Shi', 'Chenhao Liu', 'Qi Yang', 'Wenyi Yang', 'Dengke Bao']
abstract: BACKGROUND: The clinical efficacy of therapeutic cancer vaccines is critically limited by the inefficient in vivo delivery of tumor antigens to dendritic cells (DCs), the key regulators of T-cell immunity. METHODS: To address this issue, we developed a dendritic-cell-targeting adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector through rational capsid design. This was achieved by site-specifically inserting the high-affinity Clec9a-targeting peptide CBP-12, optimizing its flanking sequences, and introducing T491V/S662V gain-of-function mutations to synergistically enhance DC transduction. RESULTS: The resulting vector, AAV2-mut-Peptide2, showed significantly improved tropism for and gene delivery efficiency to cross-presenting cDC1s in vivo. In murine models of hepatocellular carcinoma, vaccination with this platform, encoding either a model antigen (OVA) or the endogenous tumor-associated antigen GPC3, elicited a potent antigen-specific CD8+ T cell response. This response was characterized by a substantial increase in tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, enhanced production of key effector cytokines, and consequently, potent suppression of tumor growth. CONCLUSION: Our study establishes this engineered AAV as a versatile and potent vaccine platform that effectively targets DCs, offering a promising approach for inducing robust and adaptable anti-tumor immunity.

title: Oncolytic virus VT1092M synergizes with immune checkpoint inhibitors against intraperitoneal metastases of colorectal cancer.
authors: ['Zongfeng Hu', 'Xinru Yuan', 'Shuzhen Li', 'Wenqi Liu', 'Jiajia Liu', 'Hua Zhou', 'Chunyang Sun', 'Chao Tian', 'Kaixuan Xue', 'Yiting Cheng', 'Jinyu Wang', 'Haitian Xu', 'Jianshuai Yang', 'Xiaopeng Li', 'Jingfeng Li']
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intraperitoneal metastasis is a frequent progression in colon cancer, highlighting the critical need for enhanced therapeutic approaches. Oncolytic virus (OV) therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy. The combination of OVs with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has demonstrated an enhanced anti-tumor response. METHODS: We generated the intraperitoneal-subcutaneous bilateral colon cancer xenograft model to simulate intraperitoneal metastatic colon cancer, and evaluated the systemic antitumor efficacy of the oncolytic HSV-1 virus VT1092M in combination with ICIs (anti-PD-L1 antibody and anti-CTLA-4 antibody). RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Intraperitoneal administration of VT1092M markedly suppressed intraperitoneal cancer progression and enhanced the superior antitumor efficacy of ICIs immunotherapy in murine intraperitoneal metastatic colon cancer. Notably, treatment of VT1092M combined with anti-CTLA-4 antibody could eliminate both intraperitoneal metastases and subcutaneous tumors, while also inhibiting the formation of peritoneal blood vessels and malignant ascites. The synergistic combination of VT1092M and anti-CTLA-4 elicited potent intraperitoneal and systemic antitumor immunity, culminating in durable, tumor-specific memory that significantly prolonged survival in mice with colorectal intraperitoneal metastases compared to either monotherapy. Mechanistically, the combination therapy activates the anti-tumor immune environment within the peritoneal cavity, leading to a significant increase in tumoricidal CD8+ T cells and M1 macrophages, as well as the reprogramming of transcriptional signatures associated with the tumor immune response within the tumor microenvironment. Ultimately, intraperitoneal immunotherapy with VT1092M enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade in suppressing intraperitoneal metastatic colorectal cancer and induces durable tumor-specific immune memory, thereby exerting substantial anti-tumor effects. This finding highlights the potential of synergistically combining oncolytic viruses with ICIs to advance immunotherapeutic strategies for intraperitoneal metastatic colorectal cancer.

title: Global trends and knowledge evolution of tertiary lymphoid structures in cancer immunotherapy: a bibliometric and visualization analysis.
authors: ['Yanan Li', 'Zhi Cao', 'Jingru Zhou', 'Yang Zhang', 'Weidong Han', 'Zhiqiang Wu']
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) are ectopic immune aggregates that arise in non-lymphoid tissues during chronic inflammation, including cancer. Their reported associations with antitumor immunity and immune-checkpoint blockade have prompted rapid growth of the field. We therefore mapped the literature on TLSs in cancer immunotherapy over the prespecified period from January 1, 2000 through March 31, 2026. METHODS: The primary bibliometric corpus comprised 1,373 English-language articles and reviews from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC). PubMed and Scopus were searched independently for descriptive comparison and were not merged with the WoSCC corpus. Analyses used bibliometrix, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, SCImago Graphica, and Microsoft Excel. RESULTS: Publication output rose markedly after 2019 and reached 315 publications in 2025. China, the United States, and France were the leading corresponding-author countries/regions, while INSERM, Sun Yat-sen University, and Fudan University led the distinct-document institutional count. Major mapped themes included B cells, immune-checkpoint blockade, spatial pathology, prognostic modeling, the tumor microenvironment, lymphatic vessels, and high endothelial venules. The independently retrieved PubMed and Scopus datasets showed broadly similar aggregate temporal and title/abstract term profiles. CONCLUSION: The analysis describes the growth, collaboration structure, and thematic development of TLS research in cancer immunotherapy. These bibliometric patterns indicate research attention; they do not establish biological mechanisms, biomarker performance, therapeutic efficacy, or clinical utility.

title: Locoregional-systemic combination therapy reshapes the treatment landscape of intermediate and advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
Addressing current challenges in cancer immunotherapy with mathematical and computational modeling
authors: ['Anna Konstorum', 'Anthony T. Vella', 'Adam J. Adler', 'Reinhard Laubenbacher']
abstract: The goal of cancer immunotherapy is to boost a patient's immune response to a tumor. Yet, the design of an effective immunotherapy is complicated by various factors, including a potentially immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, immune-modulating effects of conventional treatments, and therapy-related toxicities. These complexities can be incorporated into mathematical and computational models of cancer immunotherapy that can then be used to aid in rational therapy design. In this review, we survey modeling approaches under the umbrella of the major challenges facing immunotherapy development, which encompass tumor classification, optimal treatment scheduling, and combination therapy design. Although overlapping, each challenge has presented unique opportunities for modelers to make contributions using analytical and numerical analysis of model outcomes, as well as optimization algorithms. We discuss several examples of models that have grown in complexity as more biological information has become available, showcasing how model development is a dynamic process interlinked with the rapid advances in tumor-immune biology. We conclude the review with recommendations for modelers both with respect to methodology and biological direction that might help keep modelers at the forefront of cancer immunotherapy development.

title: Optimal control in cancer immunotherapy by the application of particle swarm optimization
abstract: In this article, a well-known mathematical model of cancer immunotherapy is discussed and used to represent therapeutic protocols for cancer treatment. The optimal control problem is formulated based on the Pontryagin maximum principle to deal with adoptive cellular immunotherapy, then the problem has been solved by the application of particle swarm optimization (PSO) in combination with regular methods of solutions to optimal control problems. The results are compared with those of other researchers. It is explained how the PSO algorithm could be enlisted to obtain the optimal controls, then the obtained optimal controls are demonstrated to be more appropriate to the elimination of cancer cells by using fewer amounts of external sources of medicine.

title: Approximate Analytical Solution of a Cancer Immunotherapy Model by the Application of Differential Transform and Adomian Decomposition Methods
abstract: Immunotherapy plays a major role in tumour treatment, in comparison with other methods of dealing with cancer. The Kirschner-Panetta (KP) model of cancer immunotherapy describes the interaction between tumour cells, effector cells and interleukin-2 which are clinically utilized as medical treatment. The model selects a rich concept of immune-tumour dynamics. In this paper, approximate analytical solutions to KP model are represented by using the differential transform and Adomian decomposition. The complicated nonlinearity of the KP system causes the application of these two methods to require more involved calculations. The approximate analytical solutions to the model are compared with the results obtained by numerical fourth order Runge-Kutta method.

title: Turing pattern induced by cross-diffusion in cancer immunotherapy model
abstract: In this paper, we investigate a mathematical model describing the interactions between effector cells (E), cancer cells (T), and the IL-2 compound (IL). The model considered here is a generalization, taking into account some cross-diffusion effects, of a spatial cancer immunotherapy model proposed by S. Suddin et al in 2021. These modifications allow us to describe two biologically relevant scenarios: a patient treated with Adoptive Cell Immunotherapy (ACI) and a patient not receiving any treatment/therapy. Cross-diffusion effects are particularly relevant in the interactions between tumor cells and the immune system, in fact they play a key role in immune response dynamics and cannot be neglected. We analyze the equilibrium points of the homogeneous system, along with their stability and bifurcation mechanisms. Furthermore, adopting the Turing approach for reaction-diffusion systems, we investigate the diffusion-driven instability and the emergence of spatial regular structures (stationary in time), i.e. the patterns. Finally, numerical simulations based on the Finite Difference Method (FDM) are presented for the two previously mentioned scenarios.

title: T cell equation as a conceptual model of T cell responses for maximizing the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy
authors: ['Haidong Dong', 'Yiyi Yan', 'Roxana S. Dronca', 'Svetomir N. Markovic']
abstract: Following antigen stimulation, the net outcomes of a T cell response are shaped by integrated signals from both positive co-stimulatory and negative regulatory molecules. Recently, the blockade of negative regulatory molecules (i.e. immune checkpoint signals) demonstrates therapeutic effects in treatment of human cancer, but only in a fraction of cancer patients. Since this therapy is aimed to enhance T cell responses to cancers, here we devised a conceptual model by integrating both positive and negative signals in addition to antigen stimulation. A digital range of adjustment of each signal is formulated in our model for prediction of a final T cell response. This model allows us to evaluate strategies in order to enhance antitumor T cell responses. Our model provides a rational combination strategy for maximizing the therapeutic effects of cancer immunotherapy.

Cardiac xenotransplantation: from concept to clinical reality.
authors: ['Ahmed A Abdelrehim', 'W Hampton Gray', 'Robert A Sorabella', 'Matthew G Broyles', 'Farshad Ghanbari', 'Charlie Hughes', 'Lindsay Johnson', 'Luz A Padilla']
abstract: Advanced heart failure afflicts over 6 million adults in the United States alone, yet fewer than 4,000 donor hearts become available for transplantation each year. Mechanical circulatory support devices extend survival for many of these patients, but device-related complications, anatomic contraindications, and limited applicability to certain populations leave a substantial unmet need. For decades, xenotransplantation (XTx)-the transplantation of organs across species-has been proposed as a means of closing this gap. The discovery of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, improved immunosuppressive strategies, and refined preclinical models have accelerated the field at an unprecedented pace. Multi-gene-edited porcine donors now survive for more than 200 days in orthotopic non-human primate models, and two compassionate-use pig-to-human cardiac transplants at the University of Maryland (2022 and 2023) demonstrated the feasibility of clinical cardiac XTx for the first time. Parallel progress in kidney XTx has yielded the first FDA-cleared investigational new drug application and the initiation of a formal clinical trial in late 2025. In May 2026, the FDA granted clearance for the first-ever cardiac XTx clinical trial (EXPRESS), using a 10-gene-edited porcine heart. The 2026 International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation Consensus Statement now provides a structured framework for recipient selection, immunologic assessment, and outcome benchmarking in cardiac XTx. Antibody-mediated rejection remains the dominant barrier, as both clinical cases ended in xenograft failure driven by antipig antibody responses despite aggressive immunosuppression. Porcine cytomegalovirus reactivation, coagulation dysregulation, and xenograft overgrowth represent additional obstacles that demand resolution before broader clinical application. The optimal immunosuppressive regimen for human recipients has yet to be defined, and long-term zoonotic surveillance protocols require further standardization. With the first cardiac XTx clinical trial now cleared by the FDA, the field continues to face not only the remaining immunologic and virologic hurdles but also the ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations that will shape how this therapy is introduced. This review synthesizes the historical, scientific, and clinical foundations of cardiac XTx, appraises the current evidence, and outlines the path toward responsible clinical translation.

title: Precision Medicine in Sickle Cell Disease: From Molecular Pathways to Curative Strategies.
authors: ['Dina Tluli', 'Omar Tluli', 'Abdelrahman A Karen', 'Mahd M Abujbara', 'Omar Sorour', 'Alaa Abdelhamid', 'Dahab Ghith', 'Mohamed A Yassin']
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a monogenic β-globin disorder characterized by hemoglobin S polymerization, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion, yet it exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity. Despite advances in supportive care and disease-modifying therapies, substantial variability in severity, treatment response, and long-term outcomes persists. Therefore, this review aims to examine the biological and clinical foundations of precision medicine in SCD, emphasizing genomic modifiers, molecular pathways, and phenotype-driven therapeutic strategies. Key pathogenic pathways including hemoglobin polymerization, vascular adhesion, and inflammatory and oxidative amplification have enabled the development of targeted agents such as hydroxyurea, voxelotor, crizanlizumab, and L-glutamine, each demonstrating domain-specific targets. Pharmacogenomic insights, particularly involving fetal hemoglobin regulatory loci (e.g. BCL11A and HBS1L-MYB), further elucidate variability in disease expression and therapeutic response. Emerging curative approaches, including allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, lentiviral gene addition, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing, represent transformative applications of precision hematology. Collectively, these advances support a paradigm shift from generalized symptom management toward biologically informed, individualized care. Continued integration of genomic profiling, biomarker stratification, and equitable implementation frameworks will be essential to translate precision strategies into sustainable improvements in global SCD outcomes.

title: Beyond Viruses: Transposons and CRISPR-Programmable Nonviral Systems for Genome Engineering.
abstract: Human gene therapy has been transformed by repurposing mobile genetic elements as tools for efficient gene delivery and precise genome modification. Viruses, transposons, and retrotransposons mobilize genetic material through distinct mechanisms with distinct advantages for genome engineering platforms with therapeutic potential. This review describes the mechanisms, performance characteristics, and translational relevance of nonviral methods of gene transfer and genome engineering, with emphasis on engineered systems such as the Sleeping Beauty (SB) and piggyBac (PB) DNA transposons, R2 retrotransposon-based platforms, CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs), and prime editing (PE). Clinical trials using both SB- and PB-engineered cells have shown feasibility by demonstrating sustained therapeutic effect through stable transgene integration, such as CD19-directed CAR-T cell therapy for hematological malignancies. These transposon-based vectors enable robust gene transfer for cell engineering, but are fairly promiscuous with respect to where in the genome they insert their genetic cargo. On the contrary, R2-derived systems and CASTs represent promising technologies for programmable insertion, but are still under preclinical development. CRISPR-based PE provides a distinct route to precise sequence correction without double-strand breaks and is particularly attractive for the correction of monogenic disorders. Taken together, these technologies define a continuum from natural genome mobility to clinically relevant genome engineering. Continued optimization of delivery, targeting, and editing fidelity will determine how rapidly these approaches move from experimental innovation into routine clinical use.

title: Restoration of infectivity-virulence and toxin biosynthesis in Botrytis cinerea B459 via upstream-targeted marker-free CRISPR/Cas9 editing of the transcription factor Bcin04g03490.
authors: ['Víctor Coca-Ruiz', 'David Saborido-Torres', 'Michele C Malvestiti', 'Jan A L van Kan', 'Ernesto P Benito', 'Josefina Aleu', 'Isidro G Collado']
abstract: Botrytis cinerea is a polyphagous fungal pathogen affecting a wide range of ornamental and agricultural crops. Previous studies on natural populations have revealed substantial intraspecific morphological, physiological, and genetic diversity. The field isolate B459 exhibits a distinctive mycelial phenotype, characterized by the lack of sporulation and sclerotia formation, and is unable to infect Vitis vinifera or Phaseolus vulgaris leaves, gerbera petals and tomato fruits. Genetic analysis traced these phenotypes to a mutation in the transcription factor gene Bcin04g03490, introducing a premature stop codon and resulting in a truncated protein. To further investigate the function of Bcin04g03490, CRISPR/Cas9-based strategies were employed to generate B459 transformants either carrying a functional B05.10 allele under the control of the constitutive olicC promoter from Aspergillus nidulans integrated at the niaD locus, or repaired at the endogenous locus through a marker-free approach involving targeted cleavage upstream of the repair template. In both cases, restoration of sporulation and pathogenicity was observed. Notably, complemented and repaired strains also recovered the toxin profile characteristic of the reference aggressive B05.10 isolate, including the production of botrydial (sesquiterpene) and botcinins (polyketides), indicating reactivation of key secondary metabolism pathways. These findings extend the functional scope of Bcin04g03490, demonstrating that it controls developmental processes, pathogenicity, and secondary metabolism pathways critical for virulence. Furthermore, this work provides a proof-of-concept for long-range homology-directed repair in B. cinerea at the Bcin04g03490 locus, offering valuable methodological insights for marker-free genome editing in filamentous fungi.

title: Zein-based hybrid nanocarriers for non-viral gene delivery: A review.
authors: ['Dua Alsinglawi', 'Enass Serry Moursy', 'Bilgesu Kasurka', 'Zainab Al-Quraishi', 'Vanessa Gi San Ho', 'Christine Dufès']
abstract: Gene therapy and RNA-based therapeutics are increasingly limited by the challenge of delivering fragile, anionic nucleic acids to the correct intracellular compartment. Zein, the principal maize prolamin, has attracted interest as a biodegradable, self-assembling carrier that can protect cargo and be combined with polymeric, lipidic, targeted and biomimetic components. This review critically evaluates zein-based systems for plasmid DNA, siRNA, antisense oligonucleotides and related nucleic-acid cargos. Native zein is best regarded as a protective and sustained-release matrix rather than a stand-alone high-efficiency transfection vector. In contrast, hybrid systems can add nucleic-acid condensation, colloidal stabilization, targeting and intracellular-trafficking functions through components such as chitosan, polyethylenimine, dendritic poly(l-lysine), lipids and targeting ligands. Direct evidence of endosomal escape remains limited, with only one reviewed study providing imaging evidence consistent with improved lysosomal escape. Cargo-specific evidence is strongest for plasmid DNA, with functional proof-of-concept also reported for selected siRNA and antisense oligonucleotide systems, whereas robust mRNA translation and CRISPR genome editing have not yet been demonstrated with zein-based carriers. The translational rationale for zein lies not in superior intrinsic transfection efficiency, but in route-specific protection, sustained release, hydrophobic drug co-loading and use as a biodegradable scaffold within multifunctional hybrids. Zein-based gene delivery remains preclinical and requires stronger mechanistic, cargo-specific and route-specific validation.

Development and validation of semi-quantitative FFQ according to Türkiye Dietary Guideline.
authors: ['Şerife Akpınar Şentüre', 'Şerife Ayten', 'Merve Esra Çıtar Dazıroğlu', 'Nazlıcan Erdoğan Gövez', 'Eda Köksal']
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aims to develop and validate a semi-quantitative FFQ specifically designed to assess dietary intake among Turkish adults (19-64 years), based on the Türkiye Dietary Guideline (TDG-SFFQ). The primary goal is to evaluate the validity and reproducibility of the TDG-SFFQ to ensure it accurately captures habitual dietary patterns in the target population. DESIGN: The TDG-SFFQ was administered through face-to-face interviews. Validity was assessed by comparing it with a 24-h dietary recall, while reliability was evaluated using a test-retest method after 4 weeks with fifty-six participants in Ankara, Türkiye. Daily intake means for energy, macronutrients and micronutrients obtained from both the TDG-SFFQ and 24-h dietary recall were calculated. Concordance between the two methods was analysed using the Pearson correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman plots. SETTING: Participants with adequate communication skills were recruited through digital announcements on social media and professional networks, followed by a snowball sampling method to expand the study reach. All eligibility screenings and subsequent data collection were conducted through face-to-face interviews. PARTICIPANTS: The study group consisted of adults (n 420). RESULTS: The agreement between the two methods demonstrated a statistically moderate or higher correlation for energy and macronutrients. Graphical representations for micronutrients also clustered around the mean, remaining within the 95 % CI. The reliability assessment of the TDG-SFFQ revealed strong linear correlations for energy and nutrients (p < 0·05), with intraclass correlation coefficients exceeding 0·666. CONCLUSION: In summary, the TDG-SFFQ is a potentially valid and reliable tool for evaluating dietary intake in the Turkish adult population.

title: Interactive Media Engagement Predicts Posttraumatic Distress After Community Trauma: A National Repeated Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: ['Sun Wook Jung', 'Mi Yeon Lee', 'Kang-Seob Oh', 'Young-Chul Shin', 'Dong-Won Shin', 'Sang-Won Jeon', 'Junhyung Kim', 'Eun Soo Kim', 'Se Youl Kim', 'Kwang-Yeol Lee', 'Nahyun Oh', 'Sra Jung', 'Sung Joon Cho']
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Media engagement is an important pathway for indirect exposure to community trauma, but little is known about how interactive platforms and meaning-making relate to posttraumatic psychological outcomes. This study examined whether different types of media usage, particularly interactive online engagement, predict acute and subacute posttraumatic distress following a communitylevel traumatic event. METHODS: A two-wave nationwide repeated cross-sectional survey was conducted 2 weeks (n=1,703) and 2 months (n=2,220) post-incident, using stratified quota sampling. Depressive, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress (PTS) symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, and the Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition. Analyses included chi-square tests, analysis of covariance with Bonferroni correction, and multivariable regression models. RESULTS: Interactive engagement correlated with elevated psychological distress at both time points. At 2 months, receiving information through online communities and sharing graphic content predicted greater symptom severity and higher odds of clinically significant depressive, anxiety, and PTS symptoms. Passive exposure to graphics was not associated with elevated distress and was linked to lower symptom prevalence. Personal relevance to victims and systemic attribution were also significant predictors, with media types showing clearer differences at 2 months. CONCLUSION: Posttraumatic distress following community trauma appears to be shaped more by patterns of interaction with trauma-related information than by visual exposure. Interactive online engagement may amplify psychological symptoms over time, highlighting the need for public health strategies that address interactive media environments.

title: Personalizing digital mental health: a micro-randomized trial analysis of cognitive behavioral therapy/dialectical behavioral therapy text messages to improve mood.
authors: ['Caroline A Figueroa', 'Jing Xu', 'Marvyn R Arévalo Avalos', 'Bibhas Chakraborty', 'Adrian Aguilera']
abstract: PURPOSE: Digital mental health interventions could improve population health. However, our understanding of how to improve their effectiveness through personalization is limited. We describe the outcomes of a micro-randomized trial (MRT) of a 60-day text messaging program, delivered during the final stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. We analyze the effects of 6 different types of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) messages, and examine whether socio-demographic, health-related, and contextual factors (eg, timing of sending a message) moderate effectiveness. METHODS: This secondary analysis included 373 adults aged 18 years or older (mean = 38.07), mostly English-speaking female, highly educated White individuals who reported being in good health, but having high stress and struggling to get their basic needs met. Participants were recruited between December 2021 and September 2022 through social media and a recruitment service (Health Match). We used the weighted and centered least squares method to examine the proximal effects of the text-message categories on daily mood, and whether sociodemographic, health-related factors, and the timing of message delivery moderated effectiveness. RESULTS: None of the 6 CBT/DBT-message categories significantly improved mood ratings marginally. However, their effectiveness varied based on the time of day and self-reported health. Overall, sending a message in the afternoon was more effective. However, certain message categories showed significant effects when sent in the morning among participants with poorer self-reported health, while some showed lower effectiveness when sent in the late afternoon for participants with better health. CONCLUSION: Our analysis underscores the importance of considering the time of day and individual health status when developing digital mental health interventions. These insights can help in designing more personalized, adaptive, and effective digital interventions.

title: AI and analytics in sports: Leveraging BERTopic to map the past and chart the future
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to map the body of scholarly literature at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI), analytics and sports and thereafter, leverage the insights generated to chart guideposts for future research. Design/methodology/approach: The study carries out systematic literature review (SLR). Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) protocol is leveraged to identify 204 journal articles pertaining to utilization of AI and analytics in sports published during 2002 to 2024. We follow it up with extraction of the latent topics from sampled articles by leveraging the topic modelling technique of BERTopic. Findings: The study identifies the following as predominant areas of extant research on usage of AI and analytics in sports: performance modelling, physical and mental health, social media sentiment analysis, and tactical tracking. Each extracted topic is further examined in terms of its relative prominence, representative studies, and key term associations. Drawing on these insights, the study delineates promising avenues for future inquiry. Research limitations/implications: The study offers insights to academicians and sports administrators on transformational impact of AI and analytics in sports. Originality/value: The study introduces BERTopic as a novel approach for extracting latent structures in sports research, thereby advancing both scholarly understanding and the methodological toolkit of the field.

title: Social Media and Mental Health
Understanding Social Media
The Mental Health Impact of Social Media
Mediated Mental Health Disclosure on Social Media and Perceived Social Support (Preprint)
abstract:
BACKGROUND

Balanced mental health is fundamental for every human being. To maintain good mental health, people may seek counseling from psychiatrists and disclose problems with family and friends. Increasingly, people also seek support for managing mental health problems on social media.

 OBJECTIVE

This study explored what kind of mental health problems Bangladeshi individuals share on Facebook groups and what kind of support individuals get from Facebook users.

 METHODS

I did a qualitative textual content analysis of 100 Facebook posts and 1,000 associated comments from public mental health focused groups.

 RESULTS

I found mental health problems in three categories (family-related, romantic relationship-related, and intrapersonal-related). Although the literature reveals up to five types of social support, this study identified two types: informational and emotional. I found that people who seek mental health support got more informational and positive support compared to emotional support and negative support. Positive support may encourage individuals to disclose more information on social media.

 CONCLUSIONS

Most of the individuals experienced mental health problems from spouses and parents. The group members helped the individuals by sharing information and offering advice to meet with the physicists. Some of the members also provide emotional support by showing empathy, sympathy and sharing personal experiences.

Emerging livestock science and technologies can drastically alter the projections of global food security models.
authors: ['Masoud Ghaderi Zefreh', 'Marcos E Dominguez Viera', 'Saeed Moghayer', 'Zuzana Smeets Kristkova', 'Willem-Jan van Zeist', 'Nils Bunnefeld', 'Ricardo Pong-Wong', 'Markus Dettenhofer', 'Ioannis Manikas', 'Andrea Doeschl-Wilson']
abstract: UNLABELLED: With the projected increase in the global population and food demand on a planet in climate crisis, the debate about the role of livestock continues to intensify. Animals farmed for food are both victims and contributors of climate change (CC), with animals suffering from heat stress due to CC but also being major contributors to greenhouse gas emissions (GHG). Livestock studies have demonstrated that novel breeding technologies could partly mitigate these negative effects, yet their wider implications for food security and the socio-economy are not well investigated yet. In this proof-of-concept study, we incorporate (1) the effects of heat stress on livestock's productivity and feed efficiency and (2) the use of genomic selection as a recently established novel breeding technology, into a global macroeconomic projection model (GMPM) to evaluate their broader impacts on food security. We find that both effects can drastically alter the model projections. In particular, the results suggest that novel breeding technologies can substantially mitigate the adverse effects of CC on production, food availability, land use, and GHG emissions, whilst also causing implications for the labour market. The study demonstrates the importance of integrating advances in livestock science and technology into GMPMs for better projections that inform livestock management, policy and consumer decision-making, requiring closer collaboration between livestock scientists and systems modellers. title: Multiscale Water Balance Analysis and Water Network Resilience Optimization in the Yellow River Basin.
authors: ['Tao Du', 'Zhilei Yu', 'Dengming Yan', 'Ze Yuan', 'Zhong Lu', 'Yan Xu', 'Quanlai Ma', 'Chouke Yang']
abstract: As a core region for ecological security, food production, and energy supply in China, the hydrological cycle of the Yellow River Basin is being profoundly altered by climate change and intensive human activities, leading to growing systemic water scarcity and increasingly heterogeneous hydrological processes. However, the lack of long-term and high-resolution hydrological data has constrained the accurate characterization of multilayer water exchange processes among the atmosphere, surface water, and groundwater at the basin scale, thereby limiting the development of sustainable water resource management strategies. This study integrates multisource remote sensing data with hydrological models to reveal the spatiotemporal evolution of the basin water cycle and to develop a resilience-oriented water network for sustainable management. By integrating remote sensing products such as GRACE and ETMonitor with distributed hydrological models, the study systematically evaluated the multilevel water balance dynamics of the Yellow River Basin from atmospheric precipitation to groundwater storage during 1991-2020. The results show that the remotely sensed groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) agrees well with in situ groundwater-level observations at the regional scale. The ETMonitor model performs well in estimating evapotranspiration over vegetated areas, with a validation root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.93 mm/day. The study revealed a pronounced spatiotemporal pattern of "water surplus in the west and water deficit in the east" across the Yellow River Basin, with the polarization intensifying under the combined effects of upstream climatic warming and humidification and intensive water consumption in the middle and lower reaches. Based on improved intelligent algorithms and channel topology constraints, this study proposed an optimized basin water network scheme. After optimization, the areal extent of water-deficient regions decreased substantially, water stress in the middle and lower reaches was alleviated, and both the balance and the efficiency of basin-wide water allocation improved. This research provides a quantitative basis for refined water resource management, water-saving irrigation retrofitting, and optimized planning of the national water network in the Yellow River Basin.

title: Recommendations for HIV care continuity during droughts and floods with key populations living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda: Qualitative insights.
authors: ['Carmen H Logie', 'Moses Okumu', 'Bay Bahri', 'Frannie MacKenzie', 'Gerald Pande', 'Brenda Katisi', 'Aidah Nakitende', 'Peter Kyambadde', 'Lawrence Mbuagbaw', 'Lesley Gittings', 'Caetano Dorea', 'Paul Bukuluki', 'Julien Brisson']
abstract: BackgroundClimate change and extreme weather events increasingly threaten HIV care continuity, yet evidence centering the lived experiences of key populations living with HIV remains limited. To address this knowledge gap, this qualitative study elicited recommendations for strengthening HIV service delivery during droughts and floods with young men who have sex with men (MSM) and female sex workers (FSW) living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda.MethodsThis community-based qualitative study involved semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of young people (aged 18-24) living with HIV (8 MSM, 8 FSW) and 20 key informants from community leadership, climate, and HIV sectors from May-July 2024. Data were analyzed using framework thematic analysis and organized across institutional, community, and household level strategies.ResultsThe 36 participants included 16 people living with HIV (8 MSM, 8 FSW; median age 23.5) and 20 key informants (7 women, 13 men) representing community leadership (n = 4), climate and environmental issues (n = 8), and HIV expertise (n = 8). Participants identified multi-level and interconnected strategies to sustain HIV care during droughts and floods. Institutional-level recommendations included decentralizing and mobilizing antiretroviral therapy (ART) delivery, expanding multi-month dispensing, maintaining emergency drug buffers, integrating nutritional support to address food insecurity, and equipping frontline workers for adverse weather conditions. Community-level strategies emphasized livelihood and savings initiatives, environmental management, infrastructure improvements, peer support networks, and targeted outreach during weather-related disruptions. Household-level strategies included strengthening food and water security, diversifying income sources, planning ahead for treatment continuity, and using practical transport solutions, such as bicycles, to overcome flood-related barriers.ConclusionsSustaining HIV care during weather-related disruptions requires coordinated responses that extend beyond the health sector. Climate-resilient HIV programmes should integrate service delivery adaptations with social protection, livelihood support, infrastructure investments, and community-led interventions to enable uninterrupted HIV care for young Ugandan key populations with HIV in climate-affected settings.

title: CRISPR genome editing in food and feed crops: intellectual property challenges, global accessibility, and the Indian perspective.
authors: ['Harshit Mangal', 'Shivangi Mathur', 'Anurag Chaurasia', 'Soumya Sharma', 'Sunil Kumar', 'Rajiv Ranjan']
abstract: The ever-increasing global demand for food and feed, coupled with population growth and climate change, necessitates the development of high-yielding and stress-resilient crops. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) technology has emerged as a transformative genome-editing tool due to its efficiency, precision, and ability to generate targeted genetic modifications. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR genome editing, including base editing, prime editing, and novel Cas variants, together with emerging approaches such as epigenome editing, mitochondrial genome editing, and hypercompact Cas systems, and their applications in improving crop productivity, stress tolerance, and nutritional quality. In food and feed crops, these applications also include crop-specific priorities such as grain and nutritional quality in food crops and digestibility, forage quality, and mineral bioavailability in feed and forage crops. Particular emphasis is placed on the complex intellectual property (IP) landscape surrounding CRISPR technologies, including patents on editing systems, delivery platforms, and proprietary vectors. These intellectual property barriers can restrict research access, technology transfer, and commercialization, particularly in developing countries. The review further discusses patent limitations, licensing frameworks, and strategies to enhance equitable global access through collaborative approaches such as non-exclusive licensing, humanitarian licensing, indigenous technology development, and international partnerships. Overall, the review underscores the need to balance innovation, intellectual property protection, and global accessibility to ensure that CRISPR-based technologies contribute effectively to worldwide food and feed security and sustainable agriculture.

title: Advances in plant metabolic engineering through synthetic biology.
abstract: The challenges associated with the escalating global population and climate change in crop production and food security are substantial. This underscores the necessity for improvements in crop nutrition, yield, and resilience to environmental stresses. Plant metabolic pathways directly influence growth, nutrient accumulation, and stress responses, rendering them prime targets for crop enhancement. Advances in plant synthetic biology and gene editing are facilitating more precise modifications of genes, regulatory elements, and metabolic pathways. This review highlights the primary technologies used in plant metabolic engineering and focuses on representative examples of their implementation for crop improvement, including but not limited to CRISPR-Cas systems, multiplex genome editing, knock-in and knock-out strategies, CRISPR-mediated gene regulation (CRISPRi/CRISPRa), base editing, prime editing, RNA targeting technologies, synthetic promoters, and gene stacking strategies. Furthermore, the emerging role of artificial intelligence in the design and optimization of metabolic pathways and genome editing tools will be briefly discussed.

title: Agricultural Landscape Understanding At Country-Scale
authors: ['Radhika Dua', 'Aditi Agarwal', 'Aishwarya Jayagopal', 'Depanshu Sani', 'Alex Wilson', 'Hoang Tran', 'Ishan Deshpande', 'Bogdan Floristean', 'Neelabh Goyal', 'Ramya Cheruvu', 'Vishal Batchu', 'Yan Mayster', 'Gaurav Aggarwal', 'Alok Talekar', 'Vaibhav Rajan']
abstract: Comprehensive agricultural landscape understanding is critical for addressing global challenges in food security, climate change, and resource management. This requires mapping not just crop fields, but also vital features like trees and water bodies which form an intricate mosaic in complex \textit{smallholder} systems dominating the Global South. Previous efforts to develop such land use maps have been limited by a narrow focus on methods for field delineation only, and also do not develop robust post-processing steps essential for real-world deployment. Further, to our knowledge, no prior system for smallholder farms has been deployed and evaluated at a national scale. This work addresses these limitations by presenting the first national-scale agricultural mapping system that moves beyond simple field delineation to enable segmentation of agricultural instances like fields, trees and water bodies. Our system is refined for real-world application using novel post-processing heuristics to ensure map consistency and accuracy, and is validated through a rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation process. Fine-grained land use maps generated by our system are publicly accessible via an API at \textit{\href{http://agri.withgoogle.com}{http://agri.withgoogle.com}}, enabling a wide range of applications from precision agriculture and policy-making to advancing global sustainability development goals.

Societal actors' perceptions of intersectoral collaboration and the participation of older adults in the development of age-friendly environments.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Older adults' participation and intersectoral collaboration are central to the development of age-friendly environments. While previous research has emphasised the importance of these principles, less is known about how they are understood and enacted by societal actors in practice. This creates a need to explore societal actors' perceptions of both intersectoral collaboration and older adults' participation in the development of age-friendly environments. METHOD: The study had a participatory qualitative design. Data were collected through a World Café involving 19 societal actors in a Swedish municipal context. Participants represented several societal sectors relevant to age-friendly environments, including welfare, care, public health, governance, social sustainability, urban planning,mobility, civil society, and voluntary engagement. FINDINGS: The findings showed that participants perceived intersectoral collaboration as requiring shared societal responsibility across multiple sectors, while responsibility risked becoming unclear when no actor had an explicit mandate to coordinate, prioritise and act. Intersectoral collaboration was viewed as a way of sharing resources, yet also as vulnerable when it relied mainly on personal relationships and informal networks rather than organisationally embedded structures. Similarly, older adults' participation was highly valued when developing age-friendly initiatives, but participants questioned whether existing participation channels adequately reflect the diversity of older adults' experiences and needs. CONCLUSION: Age-friendly work requires shared responsibility across societal actors, supported by clear coordination. Personal relationships and informal networks should be recognised as valuable for enabling collaboration, but they need to be complemented by formal structures to ensure sustainability over time. Moreover, greater efforts to reach seldom-heard older adults are needed. Doing so may contribute to more nuanced and age-friendly initiatives that better reflect the diverse needs of the older population.

title: Time series evidence on air quality transitions under urban shock during COVID-19 shutdown in Delhi-NCR, India.
authors: ['Saswati Biswas', 'Samit Bhattacharyya', 'Mudit Yadav', 'Sailesh N Behera', 'Yamini Sistla Sudha']
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic and the associated nationwide lockdown provided an unprecedented natural experiment to investigate how abrupt reductions in anthropogenic activities influence urban air quality. Although several studies have quantified changes in pollutant concentrations during the lockdown, the nonlinear temporal transitions and persistence of these changes after reopening remain poorly understood. This study investigates the evolution of air quality across Delhi-NCR, India, one of the world's most polluted metropolitan regions, by examining three distinct phases associated with the COVID-19 pandemic: the pre-COVID period, the COVID period, and the post-COVID period. Daily concentrations of PM2.5, PM10, NOx, SO2, CO, and O3, together with meteorological observations from ten CAAQMS stations, were analyzed. The analytical framework combined seasonal statistical analysis, ARIMA forecasting, Pearson correlation, principal component analysis, change-point detection, and recurrence quantification analysis to characterize statistical and nonlinear dynamical transitions in air quality. The results reveal significant reductions in pollutant concentrations and pronounced shifts in their temporal dynamics during the lockdown, characterized by multiple change points and altered recurrence structures. Source-related analysis indicates that meteorological factors and secondary pollutant formation played a greater role during the lockdown, whereas combustion and non-combustion emission sources dominated before and after the restrictions. Furthermore, cross-recurrence analysis demonstrates that post-COVID pollutant dynamics remained more synchronized with lockdown conditions than with the pre-COVID period, suggesting partial persistence of environmental improvements. By integrating conventional statistical analyses with nonlinear dynamical systems techniques, this study provides a comprehensive framework for characterizing air-quality transitions and offers policy-relevant insights for sustainable urban air-quality management in rapidly growing megacities.

title: Multidimensional Cardiac Phenotyping of Daphnia magna Enables One-Hour Effect-Based Screening of Aquatic Toxicity.
authors: ['Zitong Liao', 'Zhuo Chen', 'Yun Lu', 'Dongbin Wei', 'Xian-Wei Liu', 'Yinhu Wu', 'Wen-Long Wang', 'Yarong Qi', 'Yuming Wang', 'Ren Ding', 'Hong-Ying Hu']
abstract: Operational water quality management relies on physicochemical monitoring and targeted chemical analysis, but routine surveillance covers only a prioritized subset of high-risk contaminants and does not capture biological activity from unmonitored chemicals, transformation products, or complex mixtures. Whole-organism bioassays provide complementary effect information, yet the conventional Daphnia magna (D. magna) acute immobilization end point requires 48 h. Here, we introduce D-HEART (Daphnia-based Heartbeat Evaluation and Analysis for Rapid Toxicity Screening), a microfluidic imaging and analysis framework that converts high-speed cardiac recordings into 116 descriptors spanning morphology, pumping, wall motion kinematics, and synchrony. Within the tested response space, D-HEART assigns cardiac-response classes using a six-contaminant reference library, while its Heartbeat Toxicity Index (HTI) estimates 48 h immobilization from the predicted class and phenotype. Transcriptomic profiles provided molecular context for differentiated 1 h cardiac states. Post-training Cd(II) tests across environmental water matrices tracked immobilization with greater uncertainty than in laboratory water, and two untreated industrial wastewaters showed dose-responsive HTI estimates for mixed exposures from unseen contaminant classes. By linking early physiological states to transcriptional responses and later apical toxicity, D-HEART provides a rapid, cross-time scale effect-screening layer for operational water-quality evaluation, reducing the detection window by approximately 98% relative to the conventional 48 h immobilization end point.

title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South.
authors: ['Mingxing Chen', 'Wenming Song', 'Dadao Lu', 'Yu Deng', 'Chenglong Wang', 'Huiping Jiang', 'Yuyu Zhou', 'Murray W Scown', 'Liangkan Chen', 'Jing Ma', 'Heran Zheng', 'Xuemei Bai']
abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 103 km2), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between "low" and "high" vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

title: From flood hazard to governable climate risk: An integrated framework for adaptive flood governance and the Flood Resilience and Sustainability Index (FRSI).
authors: ['Ricky Anak Kemarau', 'Siti Norliyana Harun', 'Daniel Ugih Echoh', "Zulfaqar Sa'adi", 'Zaini Sakawi', 'Marlia Mohd Hanafiah', 'Oliver Valentine Eboy', 'Stanley Anak Suab']
abstract: Climate change, urban expansion and ecosystem degradation are intensifying flood-risk management challenges worldwide. However, mitigation and recovery approaches remain fragmented across engineering, community adaptation, technology, governance and finance, limiting integrated assessment of resilience and sustainability. This study examines the reported effectiveness and implementation constraints of flood mitigation and recovery strategies, their integration of sustainability principles, and their implications for adaptive governance. A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 62 studies combines thematic synthesis, comparative framework analysis and semi-quantitative evidence mapping. Strategies are compared across cases using reported effectiveness, implementation cost and complexity, scalability, and sustainability contributions. Standardised evidence-mapping scores support contextual interpretation rather than pooled effect estimates or universal rankings. The synthesis identifies three recurring patterns. First, hybrid approaches combine engineered protection, ecological buffering, early warning and community preparedness, with outcomes dependent on local conditions, maintenance and institutional capacity. Second, fragmented responsibilities, weak enforcement, financing constraints and limited community participation impede implementation and recovery. Third, existing assessment frameworks provide incomplete integration of physical, social, ecological, technological, institutional and financial dimensions. These findings inform the proposed Flood Resilience and Sustainability Index (FRSI), a conceptual framework comprising seven domains: hazard and exposure, vulnerability and equity, infrastructure resilience, ecological and nature-based resilience, governance capacity, technological readiness, and recovery-financial capacity. Its contribution lies in organizing these interdependent domains within a common structure for future resilience assessment and policy prioritization; operationalisation and empirical validation remain necessary. The synthesis supports coordinated institutional responsibilities, enforceable risk-sensitive land-use planning, sustained investment in complementary structural and nature-based measures, and equitable access to preparedness and recovery finance. These priorities connect flood-risk reduction with inclusive recovery and long-term adaptation.
keywords: ['Adaptive flood governance', 'Disaster recovery', 'Flood resilience', 'Flood resilience and sustainability index', 'Nature-based solutions', 'Resilience finance']

title: IoT Applications in Urban Sustainability
abstract: Internet of Things is one of the driving technologies behind the concept of Smart Cities and is capable of playing a significant role in facilitating urban sustainable development. This chapter explores the relationship between three core concepts namely Smart Cities, Internet of Things and Sustainability; thereby identifying the challenges and opportunities that exist in the synergistic use of Internet of Things for sustainability, in the Smart Cities context. Moreover, this chapter also presents some of the existing use cases that apply Internet of Things for urban sustainable development, also presenting the vision for these applications as they continue to evolve in and adapt to the real world scenario. It is because of the interdisciplinary nature of these applications that a clear comprehension of the associated challenges becomes quintessential. Study of challenges and opportunities in this area shall facilitate collaboration between different sectors of urban planning and optimize the utilization of Internet of Things for sustainability.

title: State of the Art Survey of Deep Learning and Machine Learning Models for Smart Cities and Urban Sustainability
abstract: Deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) methods have recently contributed to the advancement of models in the various aspects of prediction, planning, and uncertainty analysis of smart cities and urban development. This paper presents the state of the art of DL and ML methods used in this realm. Through a novel taxonomy, the advances in model development and new application domains in urban sustainability and smart cities are presented. Findings reveal that five DL and ML methods have been most applied to address the different aspects of smart cities. These are artificial neural networks; support vector machines; decision trees; ensembles, Bayesians, hybrids, and neuro-fuzzy; and deep learning. It is also disclosed that energy, health, and urban transport are the main domains of smart cities that DL and ML methods contributed in to address their problems.

title: Multivariate Modeling for Sustainable and Resilient Infrastructure Systems and Communities
abstract: Sustainability and resilience of urban systems are multifaceted concepts, requiring information about multiple system attributes to adequately evaluate and characterize. However, despite the scientific consensus on the multivariate nature of these concepts, many of the existing techniques to model urban sustainability and resilience are unidimensional in nature, focusing on a characterizing a single element of highly interconnected urban systems. We champion a paradigm shift in modeling urban sustainability and resilience, using an integrated approach to simultaneously estimate multiple interconnected (correlated) system attributes of sustainability and resilience as a function of key environmental factors. We present a novel case study and review a few recent studies to illustrate the applicability and benefits of the multivariate approach to modeling urban sustainability and resilience. Our proposed framework can be utilized by infrastructure managers, urban planners, and researchers to conceptualize and assess urban sustainability and resilience more holistically, and to better understand the key factors in advancing the sustainability and resilience of infrastructure systems.

title: How are cities pledging net zero? A computational approach to analyzing subnational climate strategies
abstract: Cities have become primary actors on climate change and are increasingly setting goals aimed at net-zero emissions. The rapid proliferation of subnational governments "racing to zero" emissions and articulating their own climate mitigation plans warrants closer examination to understand how these actors intend to meet these goals. The scattered, incomplete and heterogeneous nature of city climate policy documents, however, has made their systemic analysis challenging. We analyze 318 climate action documents from cities that have pledged net-zero targets or joined a transnational climate initiative with this goal using machine learning-based natural language processing (NLP) techniques. We use these approaches to accomplish two primary goals: 1) determine text patterns that predict "ambitious" net-zero targets, where we define an ambitious target as one that encompasses a subnational government's economy-wide emissions; and 2) perform a sectoral analysis to identify patterns and trade-offs in climate action themes (i.e., land-use, industry, buildings, etc.). We find that cities that have defined ambitious climate actions tend to emphasize quantitative metrics and specific high-emitting sectors in their plans, supported by mentions of governance and citizen participation. Cities predominantly emphasize energy-related actions in their plans, particularly in the buildings, transport and heating sectors, but often at the expense of other sectors, including land-use and climate impacts. The method presented in this paper provides a replicable, scalable approach to analyzing climate action plans and a first step towards facilitating cross-city learning.

title: Visual anemometry: physics-informed inference of wind for renewable energy, urban sustainability, and environmental science
authors: ['John O. Dabiri', 'Michael F. Howland', 'Matthew K. Fu', 'Roni H. Goldshmid']
abstract: Accurate measurements of atmospheric flows at meter-scale resolution are essential for a broad range of sustainability applications, including optimal design of wind and solar farms, safe and efficient urban air mobility, monitoring of environmental phenomena such as wildfires and air pollution dispersal, and data assimilation into weather and climate models. Measurement of the relevant microscale wind flows is inherently challenged by the optical transparency of the wind. This review explores new ways in which physics can be leveraged to "see" environmental flows non-intrusively, that is, without the need to place measurement instruments directly in the flows of interest. Specifically, while the wind itself is transparent, its effect can be visually observed in the motion of objects embedded in the environment and subjected to wind -- swaying trees and flapping flags are commonly encountered examples. We describe emerging efforts to accomplish visual anemometry, the task of quantitatively inferring local wind conditions based on the physics of observed flow-structure interactions. Approaches based on first-principles physics as well as data-driven, machine learning methods will be described, and remaining obstacles to fully generalizable visual anemometry will be discussed.

title: Urban Sustainability Deficits: The Urban Non-Sustainability Index (UNSI) as a Tool for Urban Policy
abstract: <jats:p>Urban sustainability has been revealed as one of the key elements in achieving global sustainability. There is a wide range of indicators in this field; however, sustainability indicators have not been exempt from criticism, in both their formal aspects and practical usefulness. If measuring sustainability is “measuring the immeasurable”, then the objective of this article is to propose a composite indicator that evaluates only the deficits of sustainability or, which is the same thing, the unsustainability of cities. This focus has the advantage of showing up the particular deficiencies and thus the priorities that each city must attend to. For this purpose, only unsustainability, defined as the distance to a sustainability target, was considered. Aggregation was carried out through generalized means, which lead to a proper balance between compensatory and non-compensatory aggregation. The results emerging from the application of our methodology to a sample of fifty different cities suggest that all cities should attend to some aspect concerning sustainability, and that no city is sustainable, but only less unsustainable, showing both significant differences between cities in terms of the degree of unsustainability and a common underlying structure of unsustainability in which the environmental dimension contributes the most.</jats:p>

Cyano-Functionalized p-Aramid Copolymer Fibers Enabling Intrinsic Rubber Adhesion for Electric-Vehicle Hose Reinforcement.
authors: ['Juyoung Kim', 'Min Woo Kim', 'Jaegeun Lyu', 'Donghoon Lee', 'Howon Choi', 'Sunjae Hwang', 'Junhyoung Jo', 'Seung Goo Lee', 'Ji Ho Youk', 'Youngho Eom', 'Han Gi Chae']
abstract: The transition to electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified durability demands on rubber hoses used for battery thermal management and coolant circulation, where para-aramid (p-aramid) fibers serve as the reinforcement of choice owing to their high strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance. However, the chemically inert surface of p-aramid fibers necessitates a hazardous resorcinol-formaldehyde-latex treatment to achieve adequate rubber adhesion, raising environmental and processing concerns. Here, we report cyano-functionalized p-aramid copolymer (CN-pAC) fibers, synthesized by copolymerizing a cyano-functionalized monomer (3,4'-ODA-CN) into the aramid backbone via in situ polymerization. The cyano groups enhanced spinning-dope homogeneity and improved fiber drawability, yielding fibers with a tensile strength of 3.63 GPa and a modulus of 90.9 GPa. The surface-accessible cyano groups increased both the polar and dispersive components of surface energy, raising the total surface energy from 23.2 to 27.7 mJ m-2. Without any surface treatment, the interfacial shear strength increased from 2.96 to 4.66 MPa with polar ethylene acrylic elastomer (AEM) rubber and from 2.39 to 3.65 MPa with nonpolar silicone rubber. This enhanced adhesion shifted the failure mode of AEM rubber-impregnated strands from fiber pull-out to fiber fracture, boosting strand tensile strength from 0.92 to 1.38 GPa. These results establish a surface-treatment-free strategy for durable aramid-rubber composites in next-generation EV components.

title: Solvation-Equilibrium Locking Enables Ultrawide-Temperature Operation of High-Voltage Lithium-Metal Batteries.
authors: ['Qingyu Dong', 'Nan Chen', 'Yang Li', 'Li Li', 'Xingjiang Liu', 'Feng Wu', 'Renjie Chen']
abstract: High-energy lithium metal batteries are promising for space, polar, deep-sea, and other extreme environments, but their operation is constrained by temperature-sensitive ion transport, Li+ solvation, and interfacial chemistry. A solvation-equilibrium-locked electrolyte (SELE) is reported by combining dimethyl sulfite (DMS), a low-freezing weakly solvating solvent, with Pyr13DFOB (1-methyl-1-propylpyrrolidinium difluoro(oxalato)borate) as an ionic-liquid co-solvent. Cooperative ion-dipole and weak C-H⋯O interactions between DMS and Pyr13 + regulate the free-solvent reservoir, while TFSI- (bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide) and DFOB- enrich the primary Li+ coordination shell. Variable-temperature 7Li NMR, Raman, and molecular dynamics simulations show that solvent-separated ion pairs, contact ion pairs, and aggregates remain nearly invariant from -60°C to 60°C, unlike the strongly temperature-responsive Pyr13DFOB-free electrolyte. This locked anion-rich solvation structure reduces solvent coordination around Li+, mitigates solvent-derived interfacial decomposition and gas evolution, and promotes LiF- and borate-rich interphases on Li metal and NMC811. Consequently, Li||NMC811 cells deliver discharge capacity at -85°C and operate up to 120°C, while pouch cells remain functional after cooling to -122.9°C. A 6.6 Ah Li||Ni90 pouch cell further achieves 565 Wh kg-1 under lean-electrolyte conditions, establishing solvation-equilibrium locking as a molecular design principle for lithium metal batteries operating over a broad temperature range.

title: Baseline techno-economic and life cycle assessment of black mass production.
authors: ['Tanongsak Yingnakorn', 'Chatisa Kansomket', 'Chaiyasit Longbutsri', 'Sean Scott', 'Tapany Patcharawit', 'Jake M Yang', 'Andrew P Abbott', 'Sakhob Khumkoa']
abstract: Recycling lithium-ion batteries hinges on economically producing black mass-the electrode powder concentrate that feeds downstream metal recovery-yet public baselines pairing real process economics with environmental impacts remain scarce. Here we show that a purely mechanical flowsheet-shredding, zigzag air classification, and circular screen vibration-applied identically to two structurally distinct feedstocks recovers black mass at 93.28 wt % separation efficiency from electric-vehicle modules and 75.77 wt % from mobile phone cells. Built on measured pilot data, loaded processing costs of $0.31-0.73/kg yield net profits of $4.39-5.53/kg under realistic feedstock purchase prices, with a probability of unprofitability below 0.2% across simulated market scenarios. Life cycle assessment attributes most impacts to grid electricity, with a global warming potential of 0.210-0.241 kg CO2 eq./kg input; a low-carbon grid cuts this by 62.8%. This paired baseline enables benchmarking of emerging recycling routes and supports circular battery supply chains.
